newsitem.title: USA: Coffee futures soar, lumber and wheat also rise.
newsitem.headline: Coffee futures soar, lumber and wheat also rise.

text.p: Coffee futures rose on Wednesday as concerns about this year's supplies heated up and tight roaster stockpiles of coffee fed buying.

In other markets, wheat and lumber prices also rose on indications that demand was picking up. Overall, the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau Index of 17 commodity futures ended up 0.17 point at 245.66 points.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee for May delivery closed up 7.55 cents a pound at 186.85 cents.
"Stocks have only moved up marginally and producers are virtually sold out," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "People believe this market is happening again."

Coffee prices hit 2-1/2 year highs earlier this month, doubling since early December as expected new crop coffee shipments from Central America and Colombia were delayed by crop damage and labor strikes.
But a steady pickup in shipments by producers in recent weeks took some of the edge off supply worries that had forced coffee roasters like Folgers and Starbucks to raise prices.

After hitting a high of 209.50 cents on March 5, May coffee had fallen back to 158.65 cents on Monday as traders took profits. But lack of more selling of futures by coffee-producing nations has sparked renewed speculative buying.
The Association of Coffee Producing Countries said in its latest monthly report that supply prospects for arabica "mild" coffee in the third quarter of 1997 look tight and vulnerable to disruptions.
ACPC estimated that coffee availability could fall to 17.91 million 132-pound bags in the third quarter of 1997 from 18.37 million in the same quarter a year earlier.

"There is going to be incredibly tight supplies," said Allendale analyst Jim Cordier. "Fundamentals show conditions are just as tight as when the market reached the highs three weeks ago. And I expect them to hit those highs again."

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, optimism that cash lumber prices will start to rise soon as spring weather boosts construction sent futures higher. May lumber closed up $8.50 per thousand board feet at $381.40.
"There is better cash market activity and the hope that it's more than a one-day wonder, which is all we had so far this year," said Curt Cunningham, president of Pacific Futures Trading.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat futures ended higher on reports that India had bought 1 million metric tons of wheat from Australia, a sign of continuing strong demand.
May wheat closed 6 cents a bushel higher at $3.95-1/2.
Traders also cited dry weather in the hard red winter wheat growing areas of the High Plains and possible delays in spring wheat seeding due to threatening floods in the Dakotas.
May corn also closed higher at $3.05-1/4 a bushel, up 3 cents, with active corn exports and talk of expanding hog production to make up for Taiwan's halted pork exports.

"There is some fear that this hog (herd) number could be a little bit bigger than people think," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities, referring to a quarterly pig crop estimate due Thursday from the Agriculture Department.
May soybeans closed down 1 cent a bushel at $8.41 as traders awaited the government's spring planting estimates due next Monday.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline prices fell as a jump in refining rates in weekly industry supply reports made the market nervous that overproduction may be ahead.
April unleaded gasoline closed 1.70 cents a gallon lower at 64.82 cents.
Refinery "run" rates in the week ended March 21 rose a sharp 2.3 percentage points from a week earlier to 92.7 percent of capacity, the American Petroleum Institute said.
The fall in gasoline led crude oil down, even though the jump in refinery rates means a greater demand -- and thus a higher price -- for oil in the short term.
"Gasoline is half of the barrel and it can steer the direction of the oil complex in the near term," said Jim Ritterbusch, a trader at Sweeney Oil in Chicago.
May crude oil closed down 35 cents a barrel at $20.64 and April heating oil down 1.40 cents a gallon at 55.43 cents.
